clinicalPearls: An aggressive clonal myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm of early childhood
Presents with hepatosplenomegaly, monocytosis, leucocytosis, cytopenias and often a rash
It is driven by dysregulation of the RAS pathway, with mutations in PTPN11, NRAS, KRAS, NF1 or CBL
There are associations with neurofibromatosis type 1 and Noonan syndrome (the latter can cause a self-limiting JMML-like disorder)
Hypersensitivity of myeloid progenitors to granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor is characteristic
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the main curative treatment for most cases
reference.pathophysiology: Juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia arises from constitutive activation of the RAS signal transduction pathway in a haematopoietic stem cell, through mutations in genes such as PTPN11, NRAS, KRAS, NF1 or CBL. This hyperactive signalling makes myeloid progenitors hypersensitive to granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor, driving excessive proliferation of monocytes and granulocytes that infiltrate the spleen, liver, skin and lungs. The clonal proliferation with dysplasia produces the mixed myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative picture and, untreated, is rapidly progressive.
additionalDifferentials: Infection causing reactive monocytosis/hepatosplenomegaly (for example viral)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and film showing monocytosis and immature cells
Bone marrow examination with cytogenetics (including monosomy 7 assessment)
RAS-pathway mutation analysis (PTPN11, NRAS, KRAS, NF1, CBL)
Assessment for neurofibromatosis type 1 and Noonan syndrome
redFlags: Rapidly rising white cell count and organomegaly
Progressive cytopenias with bleeding or infection
reference.prognosis: Untreated JMML is rapidly fatal in most children; allogeneic stem cell transplantation cures many, though relapse occurs, and certain CBL- and Noonan-associated forms may follow a milder or self-resolving course.
pitfalls: Mistaking a viral illness with hepatosplenomegaly for JMML and vice versa
Assuming all RAS-mutant infantile disease is aggressive
management: JMML is an aggressive RAS-pathway-driven clonal disorder of early childhood, so treatment intent is curative and centred on transplant rather than chemotherapy alone
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the principal curative treatment for most children with typical, progressive RAS-driven JMML

In CBL-mutated and Noonan-syndrome-associated JMML, a subset behaves indolently or self-resolves, so watchful waiting can be appropriate once the genotype is confirmed, rather than immediate transplant
NF1-associated JMML still requires transplant as the mainstay, alongside management of the underlying neurofibromatosis type 1
A hypomethylating agent or low-intensity chemotherapy is used for pre-transplant cytoreduction to control organomegaly and cytopenias, not as definitive therapy
Allogeneic stem cell transplantation is the definitive, potentially curative step for most children with progressive disease
Relapse after transplant is managed with donor lymphocyte infusion or a second transplant rather than treated as automatically terminal
Splenectomy has a selected adjunctive role for symptomatic splenomegaly or to facilitate engraftment, not a primary curative role
Radiotherapy has no established primary role in JMML management outside of transplant conditioning protocols
Supportive systemic care including blood product transfusion and prompt treatment of infection is needed throughout the disease course
Close monitoring for relapse after transplant is required given the availability of salvage options such as donor lymphocyte infusion or second transplant
Ongoing surveillance of blood counts, organomegaly and infection risk is needed during cytoreduction and the peri-transplant period
Children managed with watchful waiting for CBL-mutated or Noonan-associated disease need monitoring to detect transition to a more progressive course

Any child with suspected JMML should be referred promptly to a paediatric haematology/oncology and transplant centre, and genetic counselling offered when an underlying predisposition syndrome is identified
